question.en: What is a widget in Flutter?

keyPoints.en: A widget describes part of the user interface.
Flutter builds the interface from a widget tree.

answer.en: A widget is an immutable description of part of the user interface. Widgets can represent layout, text, buttons, or behavior. Flutter combines them into a tree and uses that tree to build the screen.

followUp.en: What is the difference between a widget and an Element?

commonMistake.en: Do not say that a widget is the rendered pixel or the mutable screen itself.

question.en: When would you choose StatefulWidget instead of StatelessWidget?

keyPoints.en: Use StatefulWidget when the widget owns changing local state.
Use StatelessWidget when its output depends only on its inputs.
State can also be managed outside the widget.

answer.en: I choose StatefulWidget when the widget needs to keep changing local state, such as a selected tab. I use StatelessWidget when the UI is determined by its inputs. For larger or shared state, I can keep the state in a separate state-management solution.

followUp.en: What happens when setState is called?

commonMistake.en: Do not claim that every changing value must be stored in a StatefulWidget.

question.en: What does a Flutter widget describe?

options.en: A configuration for part of the interface
A persistent object that stores mutable view state
An element that stores the rendered interface pixels
A renderer that paints a screen directly from data

why.en: A widget is an immutable description of part of the user interface.

tip.en: Flutter combines widgets into a tree to describe the screen.

question.en: Where is the mutable state for a StatefulWidget stored?

options.en: In a separate State object managed by Flutter
In the immutable StatefulWidget configuration object
In the BuildContext passed to the build method
In a static field on the StatefulWidget class

why.en: A StatefulWidget creates a separate State object that holds mutable state.

tip.en: Flutter may create new widget configurations while preserving the matching State.

question.en: In Flutter's layout model, what does a parent give its child?

options.en: Constraints that describe allowed minimum and maximum sizes
A final pixel size that the child must always use
A screen coordinate where the child must be painted
A list of sibling widgets that the child must measure

why.en: The parent passes size constraints and the child chooses a size within them.

tip.en: The parent then positions the child within its own layout.

question.en: When are keys especially useful in a changing list of widgets?

options.en: When Flutter must match an element to its new widget
When a widget needs a stable identifier for navigation
When an element should match a widget with another type
When a widget should preserve pixels after removal

why.en: Keys help Flutter match widgets with existing elements when their positions change.

tip.en: A stable value key is often enough for data-driven list rows.

question.en: A widget's build method should avoid causing side effects such as starting a network request.

why.en: Flutter can call build often, so it should describe UI rather than perform one-time work.

tip.en: Start asynchronous work in an appropriate lifecycle method or state-management layer.
